question: A fully loaded trainer and the same airplane flown solo are both slowed until the wing quits flying. Which one reaches the critical angle of attack first, and what does the answer say about treating a single airspeed as the stall speed?
source_note: PHAK ch.5 Aerodynamics of Flight, Stalls (printed p. 5-25). Handbook states a given aircraft always stalls at the same AOA regardless of airspeed, weight, load factor, or density altitude.

question: How steep does a level turn have to get before the wings are carrying three times the airplane's weight, and what does that do to the speed at which the airplane stalls?
source_note: PHAK ch.5 Aerodynamics of Flight, Load Factors and Stalling Speeds (printed p. 5-35). Bank beyond 72 degrees gives load factor 3; worked example 45 kt unaccelerated vs 75 kt.

question: A student insists induction icing is impossible on a 25 degree C afternoon because it is far above freezing. What combinations of outside temperature and humidity does the handbook actually warn about?
source_note: PHAK ch.7 Aircraft Systems, Carburetor Icing (printed p. 7-10). Figure 7-12 chart spans roughly -7 C to 38 C and notes icing is possible outside the depicted conditions.

question: Why is it hard for a pilot to tell detonation from preignition using the engine gauges alone, and what routine operating practices reduce the chance of either?
source_note: PHAK ch.7 Aircraft Systems (printed p. 7-20). States the two often occur together, both raise temperature and cut performance, and recommends correct fuel grade plus staying within temperature, pressure and rpm limits.

question: Four hours into a cross-country the airplane is far lighter than at takeoff. Should the pilot slow to a higher or a lower speed than the published takeoff-weight figure before entering turbulence, and why?
source_note: PHAK ch.8 Flight Instruments, airspeed limitations (printed p. 8-10). Design maneuvering speed VA varies with weight; example given is 100 kt heavy, 90 kt light.

question: Ice seals the static port during a climb while the pitot tube stays clear. What does each of the three pitot-static instruments show as the airplane keeps climbing?
source_note: PHAK ch.8 Flight Instruments, Blocked Static System (printed p. 8-11). Airspeed reads progressively low in a climb, altimeter freezes at the blockage altitude, VSI reads a continuous zero.

question: Rolling out of a turn onto a northerly heading in the northern hemisphere, does the wet compass get there before or after the airplane does, and how should the pilot compensate?
source_note: PHAK ch.8 Flight Instruments, Northerly Turning Errors (printed p. 8-26). Magnetic dip swings the float with the turn, producing a lead, so the rollout is started before the desired heading.

question: Rain begins reaching the ground under a cell that was building only a few minutes earlier. Which stage has it entered, roughly how long does that take, and why is this the stage to stay away from?
source_note: PHAK ch.12 Weather Theory, Thunderstorms (printed p. 12-22). Mature stage arrives about 15 minutes after the cumulus stage and is described as the most violent period of the life cycle.

question: Why is a light quartering tailwind worse for wake turbulence on final than a calm day, when the vortices themselves are no stronger?
source_note: PHAK ch.14 Airport Operations, Wake Turbulence (printed p. 14-28). A crosswind holds the upwind vortex over the runway; a light quartering tailwind is called the worst case because vortices can lie along the extended centerline.

question: A passenger who has been breathing fast from anxiety reports tingling fingers and light-headedness at 4,000 feet. What is the handbook's recommended treatment, and why is this not treated as an oxygen problem?
source_note: PHAK ch.17 Aeromedical Factors, Hyperventilation (printed p. 17-5). Lists the symptoms, says they are not hypoxia related, and gives restoring carbon dioxide (slower breathing, paper bag, talking aloud) as the treatment.

question: In a shallow turn the airplane wants to roll itself level, but past a certain bank it wants to keep rolling in. What causes the second behaviour, and what control input holds the bank where the pilot wants it?
source_note: AFH ch.3 Basic Flight Maneuvers, steep turns (printed p. 3-14). Outside wing travels farther in the same time, develops more lift, creating an overbanking tendency held off with opposite aileron.

question: The engine quits over water with no shoreline within gliding range and a boat already heading out. Which airspeed buys the most time in the air, and how does it compare with the speed that covers the most ground?
source_note: AFH ch.3 Basic Flight Maneuvers, glides (printed p. 3-23). Minimum sink speed maximizes time aloft, sits a few knots below best glide speed, and is cited for ditching at sea.

question: On a crosswind takeoff roll, why is holding just enough aileron to keep the upwind wing from rising not enough, and what happens to the landing gear if the pilot settles for that?
source_note: AFH ch.6 Takeoffs and Departure Climbs, Crosswind Takeoff (printed p. 6-7). The wing is held down so the airplane sideslips into the wind; too little aileron produces side-skipping and severe side loads on the gear.

question: Climbing away from a short strip with trees off the departure end, at what point should the flaps and gear come up, and what should the pilot be looking at until then?
source_note: AFH ch.6 Takeoffs and Departure Climbs, short-field initial climb (printed p. 6-12). Gear and flaps stay in takeoff position until clear of obstacles and VY is established; attention stays outside.

question: On a soft field the airplane flies itself off before it can safely climb. What is the pilot supposed to do in the few seconds after lift-off, and what speed has to be reached before leaving that region?
source_note: AFH ch.6 Takeoffs and Departure Climbs, soft-field lift-off (printed p. 6-13). Lower the nose with wheels clear and stay in ground effect until at least VX, because the airplane will settle otherwise.

question: What should a pilot decide before advancing the throttle so that stopping on the remaining runway is still a normal manoeuvre rather than a scramble, and how can the required distance be estimated from the POH?
source_note: AFH ch.6 Takeoffs and Departure Climbs, Rejected Takeoff/Engine Failure (printed p. 6-14). Pick a point by which the airplane must be airborne; summing POH takeoff and landing ground rolls estimates the distance needed.

question: The approach is so far off the desired glide path that corrections are getting larger instead of smaller. What does the handbook expect the pilot to do, rather than keep working the problem down final?
source_note: AFH ch.9 Approaches and Landings, Stabilized Approach Concept (printed p. 9-6). If the approach is very high or very low and cannot be stabilized, the pilot normally executes a go-around.

question: A pilot is high on final in an airplane with no flaps available. Which slip sheds altitude without letting the airspeed build, and what happens to the airplane's path over the ground while it is held?
source_note: AFH ch.9 Approaches and Landings, forward slip (printed p. 9-13). A forward slip increases descent rate without increasing airspeed and the direction of motion stays as it was before the slip.

question: After a bad bounce the airplane is nose-high and slow a few feet above the runway. Why is salvaging the landing the wrong choice, and what is the correct sequence of actions?
source_note: AFH ch.9 Approaches and Landings, Bouncing During Touchdown (printed p. 9-34). Go around immediately: full power, directional control, lower the nose to a safe climb attitude; airspeed decays fast and a stall may come before touchdown.

question: What combination of touchdown and control input concentrates the airplane's weight on the nose-wheel during rollout, and why does braking fail to help once it starts?
source_note: AFH ch.9 Approaches and Landings, Wheelbarrowing (printed p. 9-35). Simultaneous main and nose-wheel touchdown at excessive speed followed by forward elevator pressure; braking is ineffective and the airplane can pivot on the nose-wheel.

question: Pilots handling a forced landing often turn back toward the runway with too little height or stretch the glide to reach a nicer field. What underlying motivation does the handbook name behind this family of errors?
source_note: AFH ch.18 Emergency Procedures, psychological hazards (printed p. 18-2). Grouped under the desire to save the airplane, with the 180-degree turn back and stretching the glide given as typical consequences.

question: A gear malfunction leaves only the nose gear down and it will not retract. Which part of the airplane should touch first and in what attitude, and what two rollout problems is that meant to prevent?
source_note: AFH ch.18 Emergency Procedures, Landing Gear Malfunction (printed p. 18-13). Initial contact on the aft fuselage in a nose-high attitude to help prevent porpoising and wheelbarrowing.

question: What is the maximum gross takeoff weight of a Cessna 172S?
source_note: Model-specific performance data. Both handbooks are type-generic. Searched both PDFs: 'Cessna 172' appears only as a figure caption (PHAK p. 84) and in a re-engining example (PHAK p. 164); no weights are given. This figure lives in the aircraft's POH/AFM.

question: What equipment must an airplane carry to be certified for flight into known icing conditions?
source_note: Certification requirement, not a flying technique. Searched both PDFs: 'known icing' appears once (PHAK p. 234) only as an example of a limitation that may be placarded; no equipment list anywhere. Lives in 14 CFR part 23 and the AFM limitations section.

question: What is the maximum altitude above ground level at which a small unmanned aircraft may be flown under 14 CFR part 107?
source_note: Out of scope by design. PHAK p. 386 mentions UAS only to point readers at part 107; searched both PDFs and no altitude limit appears. Chosen because it shares vocabulary (airspace, altitude AGL) with answerable airspace questions.

question: After an engine failure in a helicopter, at what point should the pilot enter autorotation and what rotor RPM should be maintained?
source_note: Different aircraft category. AFH covers airplanes only; PHAK has no occurrence of 'autorotation' and AFH uses the word only to describe the rotation in a spin (p. 127, glossary p. 386). Belongs to the Helicopter Flying Handbook.

question: What are the current ceiling and visibility reported at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport?
source_note: Real-time information. PHAK ch.13 explains how to read a METAR but contains no observations. A fixed document can never answer this, which is the cleanest case for abstention.

question: What are the standard IFR takeoff minimums for a part 91 operator departing a runway without published minimums?
source_note: IFR operating rule outside both handbooks. Searched both PDFs: 'takeoff minimums' has zero occurrences. Deliberately phrased with in-scope words (takeoff, runway, minimums) so lexical retrieval will still return something.

question: What cylinder head torque value and time between overhaul does Lycoming specify for the O-320 engine?
source_note: Maintenance data. PHAK ch.7 explains how reciprocating engines work but gives no manufacturer figures; 'Lycoming' has zero occurrences in either PDF. Lives in the engine manufacturer's overhaul manual.

question: How much does it typically cost to earn a private pilot certificate in the United States?
source_note: Cost information, not aeronautical knowledge. PHAK ch.1 covers routes to flight instruction and certificate eligibility but no prices; checked both PDFs for dollar figures tied to training and found none.
